reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Mycosis fungoides is the commonest form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and usually runs an indolent course over years, evolving classically through patch, plaque, and tumour stages

Early patches are erythematous, finely scaly, and often persistent in sun-protected sites such as the buttocks and trunk (the bathing-trunk distribution), frequently mimicking eczema or psoriasis for years before diagnosis
A high index of suspicion is warranted for atypical, treatment-resistant, or variably shaped chronic dermatitis in an adult, particularly with poikilodermatous change
Diagnosis often requires multiple biopsies over time, since early histology can be subtle and non-specific; T-cell clonality studies and immunophenotyping support the diagnosis
Staging assesses skin (patch/plaque/tumour or erythroderma), lymph nodes, blood, and viscera, and drives both prognosis and treatment intensity

Skin-directed therapies (topical agents, phototherapy, radiotherapy) are used for early-stage disease, while advanced or transformed disease requires systemic and specialist haemato-oncological management
Sezary syndrome is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant, characterised by widespread redness, circulating atypical (Sezary) cells, and lymphadenopathy, and carries a poorer prognosis
Large-cell transformation, tumour-stage disease, and extracutaneous spread mark a more aggressive course and warrant prompt reassessment
reference.pathophysiology: Mycosis fungoides is a malignant proliferation of skin-homing mature memory T-helper lymphocytes, typically expressing a CD4-positive phenotype with characteristic loss of certain T-cell surface antigens. The neoplastic cells display epidermotropism, migrating into the epidermis and forming intraepidermal collections (Pautrier microabscesses), a histological hallmark. A clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement can often be demonstrated. Over time, accumulating genetic and epigenetic alterations, altered cytokine signalling, and impaired antitumour immunity allow progression from patches and plaques to tumours, large-cell transformation, and dissemination to blood, nodes, and organs, as seen in advanced disease and Sezary syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Drug eruptions and chronic contact dermatitis
Tinea corporis and other superficial dermatoses
Erythroderma of other causes (for the erythrodermic variant)
Other cutaneous lymphomas and lymphomatoid conditions
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy, often repeated, with immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement (clonality) studies
Peripheral blood examination including flow cytometry for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells
Full staging with lymph node assessment and imaging (such as CT or PET-CT) in advanced disease
Lactate dehydrogenase and other bloods to help gauge tumour burden
Lymph node biopsy where nodal involvement is suspected
redFlags: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is a malignancy: persistent, atypical, or treatment-resistant chronic dermatitis in an adult should prompt biopsy and specialist referral
Development of tumours, ulceration, or rapid progression suggesting large-cell transformation
Erythroderma with circulating atypical cells indicating Sezary syndrome
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or systemic symptoms suggesting extracutaneous spread
Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensively involved or eroded skin
reference.prognosis: Early patch- and plaque-stage mycosis fungoides is often indolent with a life expectancy close to normal, but prognosis worsens markedly with tumour-stage disease, large-cell transformation, nodal or visceral involvement, and Sezary syndrome; ongoing surveillance is needed because progression can occur after years of stable disease.
pitfalls: Labelling persistent atypical dermatitis as eczema or psoriasis for years and delaying biopsy
Relying on a single non-diagnostic biopsy to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking Sezary syndrome as a cause of adult erythroderma
Undertreating early disease or, conversely, overtreating indolent disease with aggressive therapy
Missing large-cell transformation or extracutaneous progression during follow-up
